title: A Strong Back
summary: How the spine is built and protected, and how good posture, light backpacks, safe lifting, and exercise keep a back strong.
poll: Schools should check how heavy students' backpacks are.

versions.title: A Strong Back
versions.text:
Put your hand on your back. Feel the bumps? That is your spine. It is your back bone.

Your spine is not one long bone. It is made of lots of small bones. There are 33 of them! They sit on top of each other in a stack.

Soft pads sit in the gaps. They work like small cushions. They help you bend and twist. They help you jump, too.

Your spine keeps a soft cord safe. The cord sends word from your brain to your body.

Strong muscles hold your spine up. They are in your back. They are in your tummy, too.

How you sit and stand is your posture. Sit up tall. Put your feet flat on the floor. Hold your phone up, not down low.

Is your backpack too full? A heavy bag can hurt your back. Use both straps. Take out what you do not need.

Need to lift a box? Bend your knees. Keep your back straight. Hold the box close.

Move each day. Walk, swim, and stretch. Do not sit too long. Get up and move a bit!

A strong back helps you play, learn, and grow.

versions.title: A Strong Back
versions.text:
Put your hand on the middle of your back. Can you feel a line of small, hard bumps? That is your spine, which is also called your backbone.

Your spine is not one long bone. Instead, it is made of about 33 small bones, which sit on top of each other like a stack of building blocks.

Between the bones are soft, rubbery pads. They work like cushions. They let you bend and twist, and they soak up bumps when you run and jump.

Your spine also has a very important job. It protects the spinal cord, a bundle of nerves that carries messages between your brain and the rest of your body.

Bones cannot hold the spine up alone. Strong muscles in your back and stomach help keep it steady.

The way you sit and stand is called your posture. Good posture helps protect your back. Sit up tall with your feet flat on the floor. Hold your phone or tablet near eye level, because bending your neck down for a long time can make it sore.

A backpack that is too heavy can hurt your back. Many doctors say it should weigh no more than about one tenth of your body weight. Always wear both straps, and pack the heaviest books close to your back.

When you lift something heavy, bend your knees, keep your back straight, and hold the object close to your body. That way, your strong legs do most of the work.

Try to move every day. Walking, swimming, and stretching are all great for your back. Do not sit for too long without getting up.

A strong, healthy back helps you play, learn, and grow.

versions.title: A Strong Back for Life
versions.text:
Place your hand on the middle of your back, and you will feel a line of small, hard bumps. That is your spine, also called your backbone, and it supports your body, but it also lets you bend and move.

Your spine is not one long bone. Instead, it is made of about 33 small bones called vertebrae. They are stacked on top of each other like a tower of building blocks.

Between the vertebrae are soft, rubbery discs. Each disc acts like a cushion. The discs let you bend and twist, and they soak up the shock when you run or jump.

Your spine also has a very important job. It protects the spinal cord, a bundle of nerves that carries messages between your brain and the rest of your body.

Bones cannot hold the spine up by themselves. Strong muscles in your back and stomach, often called your core, help keep it steady.

The way you sit and stand is called your posture. Slouching for a long time puts strain on your muscles and discs. To protect your back, sit up tall with your feet flat on the floor. Hold your phone or tablet near eye level, because bending your neck down for a long time makes your neck muscles work much harder.

Heavy backpacks are another common problem. Many doctors say a full backpack should weigh no more than about ten percent of your body weight. Wear both straps, and pack the heaviest books close to your back.

When you lift something heavy, bend your knees, keep your back straight, and hold the object close to your body. This lets your strong leg muscles do most of the work.

Finally, try to move every day. Walking, swimming, and stretching all help your back, and getting up after about thirty minutes of sitting keeps you from getting stiff. These habits can keep your back strong for life.

versions.title: A Strong Back: Caring for Your Spine
versions.text:
Place your hand at the center of your back, and you will feel a column of small, firm bumps. This is your spine, also known as the backbone, and it is one of the most amazing parts of the human body, because it holds up your weight while still letting you move freely.

Rather than being one stiff bone, the spine is made of about 33 separate bones called vertebrae, stacked one above another like a tall tower. Between the vertebrae are flexible discs, which act as cushions, soaking up the shock whenever you walk, run, or land after a jump, while also letting you bend, twist, and turn.

The spine also has an essential protective job. Passing through a hollow channel inside the vertebrae is the spinal cord, a delicate bundle of nerves that carries messages between the brain and the rest of the body, so keeping your spine healthy protects much more than your ability to stand up straight.

Bones alone, however, cannot keep the spine steady. Strong muscles in the back and stomach, often called the core, work like supporting ropes, holding the spine firmly in a balanced position.

Posture, meaning the way you hold your body while sitting or standing, has a big effect on the health of your spine. Slouching for long periods puts extra strain on muscles and discs, so experts suggest sitting up tall with both feet flat on the floor and raising screens to about eye level, because bending the neck down again and again to look at a phone makes the neck muscles hold up much more weight.

Backpacks are another common concern for students. Many doctors suggest that a full backpack should weigh no more than about ten percent of a student's body weight. Wearing both straps spreads the load evenly across the shoulders, and packing the heaviest books closest to the back reduces pulling.

Lifting the right way is also important. When lifting something heavy, bend your knees, keep your back fairly straight, and hold the object close to your body, so that your strong leg muscles, rather than your back, do most of the work.

Finally, regular exercise strengthens the muscles that support the spine. Swimming, walking, and gentle stretching all help, and standing up to move after about thirty minutes of sitting helps prevent stiffness. By building these healthy habits as children, students across Saudi Arabia and around the world can protect their backs for a lifetime of learning, playing, and growing.

versions.title: A Strong Back: Caring for Your Spine
versions.text:
Place your hand at the center of your back, and you will feel a vertical column of small, firm bumps. This structure is your spine, also known as the backbone, and it is one of the most remarkable designs in the human body, because it supports your weight while also allowing great flexibility.

Rather than being a single rigid bone, the spine consists of approximately 33 individual bones called vertebrae, stacked one above another like a tall tower. Between neighboring vertebrae are flexible discs, which act as cushions, absorbing the impact whenever you walk, run, or land after jumping, while also allowing you to bend, twist, and turn.

The spine also performs an essential protective job. Passing through a hollow channel inside the vertebrae is the spinal cord, a delicate bundle of nerves that carries messages between the brain and the rest of the body, so keeping your spine healthy protects much more than your ability to stand up straight.

Bones alone, however, cannot keep the spine stable. Powerful muscles in the back and stomach, often described together as the core, work like supportive ropes, holding the spine firmly in a balanced position.

Posture, meaning the position in which you hold your body while sitting or standing, has a significant effect on spinal health. Slouching for long periods places unnecessary strain on muscles and discs, so experts recommend sitting upright with both feet flat on the floor and raising screens to about eye level, because repeatedly bending the neck downward to look at a phone forces the neck muscles to support much more weight.

Backpacks are another frequent concern for students. Many medical experts suggest that a loaded backpack should weigh no more than about ten percent of a student's body weight. Wearing both straps spreads the load evenly across the shoulders, and placing the heaviest textbooks closest to the back reduces unnecessary pulling.

Correct lifting technique is also important. When lifting a heavy object, bend your knees, keep your back fairly straight, and hold the object close to your body, so that your powerful leg muscles, rather than your back, do most of the work.

Finally, regular physical activity strengthens the muscles that support the spine. Swimming, walking, and gentle stretching are all helpful, and standing up to move after about thirty minutes of sitting helps prevent stiffness. By developing these healthy habits during childhood, students across Saudi Arabia and around the world can protect their backs for a lifetime of learning, playing, and growing.

To explain how the brain sends messages to the body

questions.stem: A student weighs 40 kilograms. Based on the article, which backpack weight would most experts consider acceptable?
options: 12 kilograms
20 kilograms

To describe a famous hospital in Saudi Arabia
